HILL: Avi Mayer, great to have you with us this morning. Thank you.

HILL: Support for Israel really taking center stage in Michigan last night at the debate between Congresswoman Haley Stevens and Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, reinforcing the bitter divide in that race there just one week out from the Democratic Senate primary. The duo clashed over the pro-Israel super PAC backing Stevens and what it means for voters.

ABDUL EL-SAYED (D), Michigan SENATE CANDIDATE: The difference between us is $46 million of AIPAC spending.

I want your tax dollars spent in Michigan, to provide schools in Michigan, to build health care in Michigan, to build roads in Michigan. And I think that money sent over there to kill kids and women is the worst use of our tax dollars. And yet that's exactly what $46 million in spending will buy you.

REP. HALEY STEVENS (D), Michigan SENATE CANDIDATE: I want to see long term peace. I want to see a two-state solution. I am deeply proud to represent one of the largest Jewish populations in a congressional district in the country.

UNIDENTIFIED MALE: But no concern about the $46 million plus spent on the behalf of AIPAC that should worry people about perhaps you doing their bidding should you win this seat?

STEVENS: Well, I don't think there's much difference between super PACs going in for Abdul or super PACs going in for me.

HILL: The group chat is back.

The Democratic Party is struggling in this moment when it comes to support for Israel, right? There is a lot going on. There are a lot of understandably very strong feelings. How much is this going to dominate this particular race, Chuck?

ROCHA: Well, we have to separate some things. This is a Democratic primary. And I'm running a bunch of elections for November right now in marginal House seats and Senate seats where the actual majorities of the House and Senate will be. So, I'm doing polling and talking to those voters.

It's funny reading that this morning that the Israel or Palestine issue is not in the top ten of any general election when you ask, why are you voting? It doesn't mean that it's not an important issue in a Democratic primary, because you have a small subset of voters who are more tuned in, who care more about this issue. And I don't think this is as much around Israel and Palestine as it is about corporate money influence elections. And that really gets people upset, on top of Democratic base voters who really care passionately about this issue. And in Michigan, where you have one of the highest concentration of Arab American voters, it's even that much more of an issue.

HILL: So then to follow up for you on that, as you're saying, it doesn't mean it's not an issue, right, but it's not in the top ten that you're seeing nationwide, in larger reason --

ROCHA: In the general election.

HILL: In a general. I know, I understand in a general.

But when we look at what this could mean in the primary, right? And then depending on who you may get for a candidate, that's going to be really interesting if it plays out.

ROCHA: That's why you see so many people in here fighting each other.

HILL: Yes, in terms of what that could mean for the seat and for control of Congress.

ROCHA: And you also see here two different ideological folks lining up. You see all the establishment getting behind Haley Stevens. The sitting governor just came out, Gretchen Whitmer. The sitting senator who's leaving. You see Bernie Sanders, AOC and others with -- so you see the divide right in front of you.

HILL: So, you just set me up really well for my next question that I wanted to ask --

ROCHA: You're welcome.

HILL: Which is about that support, right? So, you have Gretchen Whitmer coming out in support of Haley Stevens recently, but then you have all these big name, very progressive Democrats, supporting Abdul El-Sayed. What matters more? Is it the more local big name or is it these big, national names coming in?

HARRIS: You know, I think it's interesting. Michigan, right, of course, is a -- it's a purple state. There was -- there was this comment from Abdul El-Sayed after the debate last night where he says, you know, electability doesn't need a $60 million crutch, right? This argument that there was a lot of outside money coming into the race. And so, I guess the argument from the progressives would be that, well, yes, she has a local endorsement, but she is also receiving outside funding, right?

And so, it's almost as if the two were sort of canceling themselves out. But as Chuck was mentioning, right, she's got the endorsement of also these national figures on the -- from the establishment, right? You think of Senator Chuck Schumer. You think of Representative Jim Clyburn sort of coming in from South Carolina. And so, there are -- this is a race with national implications because it does say a lot about where the base of the Democratic Party is kind of moving into these general elections. And then once you're towards the general election, it becomes a question of whether or not that base interest actually matters.

HILL: And just how widespread that, quote/unquote, base actually is, right? Because the base in Michigan is not the base in New York City, is not the base in Denver, is not the base in --

ROCHA: In these congressional seats.

So, Republicans are loving this moment of division within the Democratic Party, right? The fight over, are they Democrats? Are they Democratic socialists? So, some of that, of course, came up last night. I want to play how Abdul El-Sayed reacted to part of that.

ABDUL EL-SAYED (D), Michigan SENATE CANDIDATE: When it comes to the question of socialism, I'm not a socialist. I'm just a capitalist who understands how capitalism works. The biggest threat to capitalism was never the idea of government regulation, it was always monopoly.

HILL: He's responding to that. Democrats are going to have to continue to respond. Republicans want it that way, right, T.W., to respond to this idea. If you're a Democratic socialist or you're communist, there are a lot of ists (ph) that are being mixed up and sort of thrown in together that don't all necessarily go together. How -- as that's driving everything, right, is that enough to really keep Republicans off the questions about the economy, which is what people really are concerned about?

ARRIGHI: Well, in the inverse, we Republicans went through that in 2010 during the Tea Party era. And we had to talk about things that we did not want to talk about because we nominated candidates on the fringe of our party. It's hard to know what El-Sayed really believes because he deleted a lot of his past comments about defunding the police, about ICE, and how everyone's racist in law enforcement, about his support for socialist policies. Not only that, he's getting the endorsement of many of the leading socialists.

And so, we're seeing this play out with a fringe of the party is taking over the Democrats, and it's clouding the overall message, which is a great thing for Republicans because we have a great candidate in that race in Mike Rogers.

But make no mistake about it, this is going to get to be a bigger deal as this movement grows in places that aren't New York City, but the Democratic primary voters, like Chuck just said, are more in tune and have a bigger voice. You have candidates right now who Mamdani has endorsed, who were at a pro-Palestinian rally the day after the October 7th attacks, where there were people openly chanting in support of Hamas. You have people saying, America deserved 9/11. These are outrageous things that will pollute the well for Democrats.

And, yes, it's a good political thing for Republicans. I don't think it's a good thing for our country.

HILL: I also want to talk about Senator Mitch McConnell. So, we got an update from his office. This, of course, on the heels of what we're told was a fall last month.

This is not really helping the skepticism at all. So, his office releasing this picture on Monday, as well as a statement from the office of the attending physician, which reads in part, he is not yet medically cleared to leave the rehab facility and return to office.

Kentucky Governor Andy Beshear, pretty clear, that's not good enough, writing, "I understand anyone's desire for privacy, but when you run for office and serve as one of the state's two U.S. senators, you willingly abdicate much of your personal privacy." Going on to say, "I'm calling on you to directly and verbally address the people of Kentucky and provide proof" to your campaign to serve -- "of your capacity," rather, "to serve or resign."

Does Mitch McConnell need to get on board with that? I mean we do live in an era, right, where it is very easy for you to snap a video, here I am, I'm moving, I'm talking, I'm doing all the things. That's not happening.

ARRIGHI: No. And it should. I think every American wants more transparency.

Even the Republicans of Kentucky would like it. I'm not saying Mitch McConnell is lying or being deceitful. I just think he should be more forthright and put out a quick video.

But look, let's put this in perspective. He's not running again, which was a good thing. I wish we had all old politicians say they aren't running again. He's not running again. We have three, four weeks maybe of the Senate calendar left. Everything else is operating. And we have a -- they have a Democratic governor in Kentucky. So, resigning is out of the option -- out of the playbook.

HILL: Still a few weeks left, though. You're still in the job, right?

ARRIGHI: I agree. I agree.

ROCHA: Right. And I think that this also raises a bigger point of, as we have a Congress that's not that representative of the people because the average age is so much older, it's so much more male, it's so much more -- all the things that don't look like America. If we had some -- stay with me here. I'm not saying it's got to be a 55 age limit but maybe we just do 70 and say, if you get to 70, maybe you shouldn't be in Congress no more.

And my last thought on that is, I'm 57. I know I look damn good for 57, but I'm 57. It was hard for me to get up this morning to get here. I couldn't imagine being 70 and being in all my faculties.

HILL: Well, which also raises the question, is this about age, right, because there could certainly be, and valid, perhaps, questions about ageism. Is it about, you're 71, you shouldn't be there? Or is it about term limits, which is something that has, you know, been kicked around for decades here? Are we starting to see more of a push for maybe a term limit? Because this is not the first instance that we've had, right, about questions?

HARRIS: I think we are -- I think we are seeing more of a push for term limits. I also think we're seeing more of a conversation around the abilities of some, you know, some more senior lawmakers to continue to function in their positions. But I think, as T.W. mentioned at the beginning, right, this could have been solved with a little bit more transparency.

HARRIS: It takes about a minute to record your video, to post it online, to say, hi, everybody, I'm doing all right. It's -- there's an understandable bit of privacy that you would -- you would want in a situation like this. But as a representative of the people who is receiving a salary for the people who -- from the people who have voted for you, he probably does owe it to the voters to have a little bit more transparency in this case.

HILL: Chuck, you made a point about, you know, where people stand, right? You weren't saying 55. You were saying 71. You had said something earlier too, not in sort of pre-notes, right, for the show about, also, I mean, these are also, let's say, older representatives, right, need to understand what's happening in the world, that they're not representative. You mentioned a comment from a Democrat, I know, earlier --

ROCHA: All I said was a senior Democrat.

HILL: So, a senior Democrat, but it's getting a lot of attention, who was asked about A.I. I'm just going to play that --

HILL: Because I do think it's an interesting discussion point.

UNIDENTIFIED MALE: No ChatGPT. No cloth (ph) for you.

REP. JIM CLYBURN (D-SC): Believe it or not, I didn't even know what that was until about a week ago.

UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Which one?

CLYBURN: ChatGPT or whatever it is.

UNIDENTIFIED MALE: You didn't know until a week ago. Wow. I'm jealous. You kept yourself in the bubble.

CLYBURN: That may -- that may sound strange to you. I don't know -- I didn't know what that was.

HILL: It's funny in the moment, but then it's not. And Congressman Clyburn, right, quite a record.

HILL: But for him to say, I didn't know what A.I. was until a week ago, this is something that has been brought up by voters. There are concerns about it, right? They're asking their lawmakers to do something about it. The president talks about it a lot.

ROCHA: Look, my wife is teaching me how to use TikTok. I shouldn't be the one regulating TikTok. That's all I'm saying here. And folks should be -- with the way that things are moving so quickly, and as I'm making TV ads with data centers and A.I. and all the other algorithms, and things that are feeding us every day on this thing, making us hate each other and not love each other, like, we should just be a lot more tuned in because things are moving so fast and that Congress -- this ain't nothing against Mr. Clyburn or anybody else, but our Congress and our Senate is almost made to move slowly when things are moving so quickly now.

HILL: Well, you could change all that because I understand in your group chat, Chuck, there's a big push for you to be in charge of the DNC.

ROCHA: No, there was a big push. And then my -- I'm just saying --

HILL: I thought it had been renewed.

ROCHA: It had not been renewed. And I want to give -- actually come to Ken Martin's defense a little bit. For all of you out there who want a millionaire or a billionaire to be in charge of the DNC, you got a guy that's there who was actually giving out money to the state parties or opened up 60 offices in Georgia. All I was saying is, thank God I made the right decision.

ARRIGHI: I don't -- I don't think that my endorsement would help you in your run for DNC chair.

ROCHA: I don't think (INAUDIBLE). HILL: Probably not.

Today: Trump to Meet with Zelenskyy and Netanyahu; Crews Race to Contain Flames in France & Spain. Aired 6-6:30a ET

Aired July 28, 2026 - 06:00   ET

THIS IS A RUSH TRANSCRIPT. THIS COPY MAY NOT BE IN ITS FINAL FORM AND MAY BE UPDATED.

UNIDENTIFIED MALE: -- new home.

BRAD SMITH, CNN ANCHOR: I might equip (ph). Not going to lie.

And let's take you to Seattle. That's where the Internet's favorite raccoon, Jimothy, was honored in his city.

ALEXIS MERCEDES RINCK, SEATTLE COUNCIL MEMBER: Council members Alexis Mercedes Rinck and Dan Strauss proclaim summer of 2026 to be Jimothy Summer.

SMITH: Hot Jimothy Summer rolls on. Hundreds of people gathered Sunday to honor the beloved critter.

That does it for CNN HEADLINE EXPRESS. I'm Brad Smith. CNN THIS MORNING with Audie Cornish starts right now.

ERICA HILL, CNN ANCHOR: Today in the group chat, the war in Iran putting a strain on one of the world's closest alliances. So, will today's meeting between President Trump and Prime Minister Netanyahu, just what will it reveal?

UNIDENTIFIED MALE: What have you said to Prime Minister Netanyahu about Iran, and how long to hold off on strikes?

DONALD TRUMP, U.S. PRESIDENT: That's fine. He'll do whatever I want him to do.

HILL: President Trump also set to meet with President Zelenskyy today. Could the White House be changing its approach to the war in Ukraine?

Europe's wildfire crisis getting worse. Crews now scrambling just to contain the flames. Can they actually get ahead of any?

And a new picture and a doctor's note from Senator McConnell's office. But does this do anything to settle the demand for real answers about his health?

UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Why is Mitch not talking on a video? Why y'all won't let the man talk? If he is fit to sit on Congress, he should be able to talk.

HILL: Today, two high-stakes meetings and one key question. Just how will President Trump balance Zelenskyy's push for peace with Netanyahu's push for war?

Good morning, everyone, on this Tuesday. I'm Erica Hill, in for Audie Cornish. Nice to have you with us.

Benjamin Netanyahu and Vladimir Zelenskyy are in town this morning for the funeral of their key ally, Senator Lindsey Graham. But it's not the only thing on their agendas. Zelenskyy is hoping to secure anti- ballistic defense and strategic cooperation in the war with Russia, as well as new Russian sanctions that were backed by the late Senator Graham.

Now, for Netanyahu, this is actually the first time he'll be meeting with Trump face-to-face since the war with Iran began. And it comes as Trump is at a crossroads. Does he escalate the war, as Netanyahu wants, or talk things out?

BENJAMIN NETANYAHU, ISRAELI PRIME MINISTER (through translator): We will discuss all the issues on the agenda, foremost among them Iran. Of course, our goal is to safeguard our security while also expanding the circle of peace around us.

UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Are you on the same page on Iran, you and Prime Minister Netanyahu?

TRUMP: Pretty close. Yes. Pretty close. We have a little difference, but pretty close. Yes.

HILL: Today in the group chat, Adam Harris, co-host of "Radio Atlantic"; Chuck Rocha, Democratic strategist and former senior advisor for Bernie Sanders' presidential campaigns; and T.W. Arrighi, former senior communications aide to Lindsey Graham.

Gentlemen, it's nice to have all of you at the table today. We were joking. It was all ladies yesterday. Today it is all the men joining here at the table. This is a -- a big day. There is no getting around that. When we look

at the leaders who are going -- going to be meeting with President Trump. And it's certainly an interesting time for both of them when it comes to.

Let's start off with Prime Minister Netanyahu. It does seem that there's been a little bit of a strain on this relationship. The president calling him "'F'-ing" crazy over strikes in Lebanon, certainly not seeing eye-to-eye on the relationship with Turkey.

I'm curious: when they do finally meet face-to-face today, how do you expect this to play out?

ADAM HARRIS, CO-HOST, "RADIO ATLANTIC": You know, it will be -- it will be interesting, right? I think what we've seen over the last month has been that sort of increasingly strained relationship from those strikes in Lebanon that functionally ended the ceasefire agreement, that -- that had only been established for -- for a little while.

I think that what we -- what we've really -- are going to look for is whether or not, after 14 days of -- of bombing in Iran has resumed, and President Trump has sort of backed away from it, whether the president and Prime Minister Netanyahu really sort of decide whether or not, you know, this -- this is something that they're going to continue, right?

Whether they actually do want to be and sort of have that muscular attack in Iran, or if they want a more diplomatic solution to this, which has been, to this point, elusive.

HILL: And there have been questions from the beginning, right, about different -- not only different strategies, but obviously different aims for each of these two leaders when it comes to the war.

All of this playing out, as well, as we have, of course, the Ukraine issue on the table. President Zelenskyy coming in. How different do you think these meetings will be?

CHUCK ROCHA, DEMOCRATIC STRATEIGST: I think there's an anxiety at the White House and abroad over a couple of things. And let's talk about and build off of what Adam said about what's the tension.

The tension with Netanyahu is he wants to continue to blow things up in Iran as much as possible. I'm putting that in redneck terms this morning.

But the president wants it to end as quickly as possible. He may not say that, but I will promise you, him, and especially Republicans in Congress, with gas at $4.11 a gallon, they want the war to be over; so gas prices can come down, and they can concentrate on the midterms, and have some a good-faith effort to try to fight the Democrats at midterms without talking about this war that is so unpopular with Democrats and Republicans.

[06:05:04] HILL: OK. But you didn't answer my question about the difference in the meetings.

ROCHA: I was leaving that for T.W. He's a foreign expert.

T.W. ARRIGHI, FORMER SENIOR COMMUNICATIONS AIDE TO LINDSEY GRAHAM: I don't know about that.

I think, broadly speaking, that is correct. In -- in Iran and Israel. Let's start there with Benjamin Netanyahu.

Benjamin Netanyahu's worldview is that Israel is surrounded, and the Jewish people are surrounded on all sides by people who want their destruction. So, his battle will not end until those threats cease.

Donald Trump looks at it as a singular threat. Iran, who has the blood of thousands of Americans on their hands, who has been a terror to the world, who has disrupted trade for -- for many years and decades, including right now, obviously.

But the fact of the matter is for Iran, that situation will not change unless the regime itself thinks that threat, that its demise is imminent. Right now, they don't feel that way.

Where it goes from here is an open question. Obviously, Netanyahu would like a step up. People running for office would like a step down. That's an open question.

With Zelenskyy, the Russian people have suffered over a million casualties in that -- in that conflict. Zelenskyy and the Ukrainian people have held up admirably.

But more importantly, as we're looking at these global conflicts in Iran, potential things brewing in Asia, I also want to look at the technologies and the battlefield technologies that have come out of Ukraine.

So, look for President Trump to look for cooperation with Zelenskyy on those new technologies, going in both directions, to better --

HILL: Which Zelenskyy has offered. Right?

ARRIGHI: -- solidify us.

HILL: Especially since the start --

ARRIGHI: Yes, of course.

HILL: Especially since -- the drones, since the start of the Iran War.

HILL: It's also fascinating, when we look at Zelenskyy, I was spoken [SIC] with -- speaking with former ambassador to Ukraine Bill Taylor over the weekend. He said to me, too, what he sees is working in Zelenskyy's favor right now is Ukraine can point to some wins.

Donald Trump likes a winner, so that could be helpful.

There's also the question, the Laura Loomer of it all, right? The fact that Laura Loomer was in Ukraine; the fact that this may be changing, perhaps, some perspective within the MAGAverse, within more right- leaning members.

How critical do you think that is to Zelenskyy's argument and to what he's bringing into this meeting?

HARRIS: I think that that transition, right, of a lot of people in that MAGA universe sort of moving towards saying, you know, we should be supporting Ukraine, right? Russia is the aggressor here.

And that functional -- what Laura Loomer called sort of a woke right, right? She -- she referred to Tucker Carlson as a sort of woke right.

And -- and President Trump sort of approvingly sort of thumbs-upping her interview with Zelenskyy.

I think that you're right in that the recent wins that Zelenskyy has had, alongside the -- the bombing of the Iranian ship more recently, I think that -- that he is seeing it as this is someone who is projecting strength, right, in the way that that the president likes to see strength projected.

I think what will be interesting is that the fact that Russia has had this large barrage on -- on Iran [SIC], right? And on -- on Ukraine. And Ukraine is looking for these anti-ballistic missiles, right? They're looking for the -- the Patriot missiles so that they can -- they can sort of deter some of those strikes.

And so, it will be -- this is a really crucial moment for Zelenskyy and for President Trump.

HILL: What is missing now, of course, in this moment -- and T.W. this is for you for obvious reasons -- is Senator Graham, right, who was not only a very close ally. Right? And very big supporter of -- of these leaders, these -- these causes in this moment.

But he was -- I mean, he was the Trump whisperer, right? So, just before he passed, he had just come back from Kyiv; was talking about the support that he had earned, I think, finally, from the president when it came to the sanctions bill.

Without Lindsey Graham around to get in the president's ear, what does it change?

ARRIGHI: A lot. There is no natural successor to the level of influence Lindsey Graham had on the world stage, their close relationship he had with these world leaders.

The fact that they're both coming to Washington to honor him, along with a number of Senate colleagues on both sides of the aisle, says everything you need to know. So, yes, it is -- it is a huge deal. And I really hope, and I believe

fully, that his sister, who's doing a tremendous job trying to fill his shoes, will help get across -- get across the finish line those Russia sanctions that are so desperately needed.

Because like you said, Donald Trump, right when he came back from Kyiv and announced that we had an agreement, Donald Trump went along with it.

So, that's a massive, massive step forward in Ukraine. And I hope that today is a -- and today we lay him to rest and celebrate his life over the next two days is a galvanizing event to get that finished in his memory.

But make no mistake about it: his impact will be felt, the loss of it, all over the world.

HILL: All right. Much more ahead here on CNN THIS MORNING, including a major decision in the murder case against singer D4vd.

Plus, "Today Show" anchor Savannah Guthrie with a new plea for her missing mother.

And a troubling revelation about a very popular jetliner. This is widely used across the United States. The seats, the FAA says, have been installed all wrong. So, just how concerned should you be?

HILL: Fourteen minutes past the hour here. We've got your morning roundup for you.

The case against singer D4vd will go to trial. A judge ruling there is, in fact, enough evidence to move forward.

He's accused of killing 14-year-old Celeste Rivas Hernandez and will be held without bail until an arraignment on August 31st.

Savannah Guthrie, making a new plea to bring her missing mother home.

SAVANNAH GUTHRIE, HOST, "THE TODAY SHOW": I'm asking you, begging you to do the right thing now. Make the right choice. Help us find her.

HILL: It has been nearly six months since Nancy Guthrie was taken from her Arizona home.

A masked man was seen tinkering with the 84-year-old's doorbell camera the morning she disappeared. No suspects, though, have been identified in the case. Oregon's governor is now calling for state and federal investigations.

State and federal investigations have actually been opened in Oregon after reports of armed men impersonating ICE officers.

A victim was allegedly assaulted last week after the suspects pulled them over on the highway, showed fake badges. They were also wearing vests that said "Police" on them; told the person they were being arrested, searched the car, held the victim for at least 15 minutes, but then let them go.

The FAA is warning that seats on hundreds of Boeing 737 MAX jets were incorrectly installed, and the FAA says if not fixed, those seats could cause serious injury in the case of an emergency landing.

The 737 MAX is widely used by U.S. airlines. This notice from the FAA impacts more than 450 which are currently registered across the country.

The FAA did not say how quickly airlines would need to fix that issue.

After the break here on CNN THIS MORNING, we're going to take you live to Spain, where the wildfires are raging.

Plus, questions about Senator McConnell's health not going away. Why this new photo is raising even more concerns.

And a live look at St. Louis. Good morning to our friends out there. An extreme heat warning, of course, remains in effect. The real temperatures, real-feel temperatures for you guys today, around 111.

HILL: We are following breaking news at this hour out of Japan. So, this is new video just coming into us here in the wake of a 7.1- magnitude earthquake in the Southern part of the country. You see that bridge collapsed there? A shrine, part of that has toppled.

And we also have images for you that show a moat; a wall and a moat outside of a famous castle. I think we may have that, as well, which has crumbled.

We do know power has been knocked out to thousands of homes. Experts right now are warning residents about aftershocks and landslides.

At this hour, we know at least 50 people have been injured. We're going to continue to monitor that situation for you out of Japan.

The air in Bordeaux, France, raising serious concerns this morning as pollution levels are now six times above safety levels as wildfires burn with no end in sight.

EMMANUEL MACRON, FRENCH PRESIDENT (through translator): We must understand that we are facing a completely unprecedented wildfire. The situation we are dealing with today is the most severe we have ever recorded, the toughest since the Second World War.

HILL: Officials say firefighters are battling flames so intense the flames themselves are actually creating what's known as fire clouds. It's a phenomenon that has actually never been seen in France before.

And of course, we have this heat wave we've been talking about that's moving in. That could further fuel the flames.

The situation not much better in Spain, where officials say the country is now facing the largest fire in the nation's history. CNN international correspondent Pau Mosquera, joining us now with more from Spain.

Where do things stand? We can see that scorched earth around you right now. Paul.

PAU MOSQUERA, CNN INTERNATIONAL CORRESPONDENT: Exactly, Erica. Because what you can see around me is the result of the biggest wildfire ever registered in Spain.

This is the Bourgogne (ph) wildfire that started last week and has already scorched more than 50,000 hectares of land.

Just have a look to the landscape. I mean, the ground looks completely black, charred, and there's no sign of plant life. Also, you can see that most of the trees have been reduced to ashes, and some of them are still standing, but the trunks have been completely burned.

And actually, if you look behind me, you can see how the fires are still very much active. Because what you can see that seems to be a layer of haze is actually the smoke rising from the areas where there are active fire fronts, which is South and West from where we are.

And this is also the reason, Erica, why we are wearing and using these face masks, just in case the air quality keeps deteriorating any further.

Now, it is important to say that, despite this situation that we are showing you, authorities showed today a little bit of cautious optimism. Because they say that overnight, the 400 firefighters that have been working to contain this wildfire actually got to prevent the flames from spreading any further. But the fires are still out of control.

And actually, it's important, because the next few hours are going to be crucial. Because tomorrow, Wednesday, the weather conditions are expected to worsen as the fourth heat wave of the summer is going to impact the Iberian Peninsula.

And, you know, the higher the temperature, the lower the humidity, the greater the risk for new wildfires -- Erica.

HILL: Yes, absolutely. And the more difficult, of course, it is for those crews that are battling the wildfires already there.

Pau, really appreciate it. Thank you.

Still to come here on CNN THIS MORNING, the family of Kansas City Chiefs Coach Eric Bieniemy rocked by gun violence. His son now behind bars.

Plus, President Trump taking his fight over mail-in voting to the high court.

HILL: Good morning. Thanks for starting your day with us here on CNN THIS MORNING. Just about half past the hour now. Here's a look at what's happening right now.

Later this morning, the funeral for Senator Lindsey Graham will be held. Services set to be held inside the Capitol Rotunda and at the National Cathedral. President Trump is expected to deliver the eulogy.

Graham's casket will be transferred to South Carolina tomorrow for a private service.

The son of Kansas City Chiefs offensive coordinator Eric Bieniemy is being held without bond this morning after.

sentences.en: Today, two high-stakes meetings and one key question: just how will President Trump balance Zelenskyy's push for peace with Netanyahu's push for war?
sentences.cn: 今天有两场高风险会议和一个关键问题：特朗普总统将如何平衡泽连斯基的和平诉求与内塔尼亚胡的战争诉求？
sentences.structure: 简单句，冒号后为同位语解释说明。
sentences.analysis: 主干为'Today, two high-stakes meetings and one key question'，冒号后为同位语从句，解释'key question'的内容。'balance...with...'为固定搭配，表示平衡两者。

sentences.en: Zelenskyy is hoping to secure anti-ballistic defense and strategic cooperation in the war with Russia, as well as new Russian sanctions that were backed by the late Senator Graham.
sentences.cn: 泽连斯基希望获得反弹道导弹防御系统以及与俄罗斯战争中的战略合作，以及已故参议员格雷厄姆支持的新对俄制裁。
sentences.structure: 复合句，包含定语从句。
sentences.analysis: 主干为'Zelenskyy is hoping to secure...'，宾语为'anti-ballistic defense and strategic cooperation'和'new Russian sanctions'。'as well as'连接并列宾语。'that were backed by the late Senator Graham'为定语从句修饰'sanctions'。

sentences.en: And it comes as Trump is at a crossroads: does he escalate the war, as Netanyahu wants, or talk things out?
sentences.cn: 而此刻特朗普正处在十字路口：他是按内塔尼亚胡的意愿升级战争，还是通过谈判解决？
sentences.structure: 复合句，包含时间状语从句和同位语。
sentences.analysis: 主句为'it comes'，'as'引导时间状语从句。冒号后为同位语，解释'crossroads'的具体选择。'as Netanyahu wants'为方式状语从句。

sentences.en: I think what we've seen over the last month has been that sort of increasingly strained relationship from those strikes in Lebanon that functionally ended the ceasefire agreement that had only been established for a little while.
sentences.cn: 我认为我们在过去一个月看到的是那种日益紧张的关系，源于黎巴嫩的打击，这些打击实际上结束了仅建立不久的停火协议。
sentences.structure: 复合句，包含多个从句。
sentences.analysis: 主句为'I think'，后接宾语从句'what we've seen...has been...'。'what we've seen'为主语从句。'that sort of...relationship'为表语。'from those strikes...'为介词短语作定语。'that functionally ended...'为定语从句修饰'strikes'。'that had only been established...'为定语从句修饰'ceasefire agreement'。

sentences.en: I think that what we really are going to look for is whether or not, after 14 days of bombing in Iran has resumed, and President Trump has sort of backed away from it, whether the president and Prime Minister Netanyahu really sort of decide whether or not, you know, this is something that they're going to continue, right?
sentences.cn: 我认为我们真正要看的是，在伊朗轰炸恢复14天后，特朗普总统有点退缩了，总统和内塔尼亚胡总理是否真的决定是否要继续这件事。
sentences.structure: 复合句，包含多个从句。
sentences.analysis: 主句为'I think'，后接宾语从句'what we really are going to look for is...'。'what we really are going to look for'为主语从句。'whether or not...'为表语从句，其中包含'after...'时间状语从句和'whether...decide whether or not...'嵌套。

sentences.en: But the fact of the matter is for Iran, that situation will not change unless the regime itself thinks that threat, that its demise is imminent.
sentences.cn: 但事实是，对伊朗来说，除非政权本身认为威胁——即其灭亡即将来临，否则情况不会改变。
sentences.structure: 复合句，包含条件状语从句和同位语。
sentences.analysis: 主句为'the fact of the matter is...'，后接表语从句'that situation will not change...'。'unless'引导条件状语从句。'that threat'后接同位语从句'that its demise is imminent'，解释'threat'的内容。

sentences.en: But more importantly, as we're looking at these global conflicts in Iran, potential things brewing in Asia, I also want to look at the technologies and the battlefield technologies that have come out of Ukraine.
sentences.cn: 但更重要的是，当我们审视伊朗的全球冲突以及亚洲酝酿的潜在事态时，我也想关注从乌克兰涌现的技术和战场技术。
sentences.structure: 复合句，包含时间状语从句和定语从句。
sentences.analysis: 主句为'I also want to look at...'。'as'引导时间状语从句。'that have come out of Ukraine'为定语从句修饰'technologies'。

sentences.en: And that functional -- what Laura Loomer called sort of a woke right, right? She referred to Tucker Carlson as a sort of woke right.

sentences.structure: 复合句，包含插入语和直接引语。
sentences.analysis: 'And that functional'后破折号插入'what Laura Loomer called sort of a woke right'，其中'what'引导名词性从句。后一句为直接引语，解释前文。

sentences.en: The fact that they're both coming to Washington to honor him, along with a number of Senate colleagues on both sides of the aisle, says everything you need to know.

sentences.structure: 复合句，包含同位语从句和定语从句。
sentences.analysis: 主语为'The fact'，后接同位语从句'that they're both coming...'。谓语为'says'，宾语为'everything'，后接定语从句'you need to know'。

sentences.en: Because like you said, Donald Trump, right when he came back from Kyiv and announced that we had an agreement, Donald Trump went along with it.
sentences.cn: 因为正如你所说，唐纳德·特朗普，就在他从基辅回来并宣布我们达成协议时，他同意了。
sentences.structure: 复合句，包含时间状语从句和宾语从句。
sentences.analysis: 'Because'引导原因状语从句。主句为'Donald Trump went along with it'。'right when he came back...'为时间状语从句，其中包含'and announced that...'，'that'引导宾语从句。

sentences.en: On Monday, he asked the Supreme Court to allow his executive order curtailing mail-in voting and is also demanding again that the Senate pass his elections bill, even if it means killing the filibuster.
sentences.cn: 周一，他请求最高法院允许其限制邮寄投票的行政命令，并再次要求参议院通过他的选举法案，即使这意味着废除阻挠议事规则。
sentences.structure: 主句：he asked the Supreme Court to allow his executive order curtailing mail-in voting and is also demanding again that the Senate pass his elections bill, even if it means killing the filibuster.
sentences.analysis: 本句为并列结构，由and连接两个谓语动词asked和is demanding。第一个谓语后接不定式短语to allow...作宾语补足语，其中curtailing...为现在分词短语作定语修饰order；第二个谓语后接that引导的宾语从句，从句中包含even if引导的让步状语从句。

sentences.en: But the problem is this, if the high court were to agree with them, and this is an administrative state, it's not really even reaching the merits, just pause for a moment, basically the harm that the lower courts recognize is irreparable would come to pass because you're letting these actions start to get carried out without the proper judicial review as to whether they're lawful or not.
sentences.cn: 但问题在于，如果最高法院同意他们的观点，而这是一个行政国家，这甚至没有触及实质问题，暂停一下，基本上下级法院认定的不可挽回的损害就会发生，因为你让这些行动在没有适当司法审查（审查其是否合法）的情况下开始实施。
sentences.structure: 主句：But the problem is this, ... basically the harm ... would come to pass because ...
sentences.analysis: 本句结构复杂。主句为the problem is this，后接if引导的条件状语从句，其中包含插入语and this is an administrative state。主句后basically引导的句子进一步解释，其中that the lower courts recognize is irreparable为定语从句修饰harm，because引导原因状语从句，其中包含as to whether引导的宾语从句。

sentences.en: So really what they're trying to do is to fudge the request. They're saying, look, we're just saying that the district courts acted too early, but actually, if you stop what the district courts did, we basically get what we want right now.
sentences.cn: 所以他们实际上是在含糊其辞。他们说，看，我们只是说地区法院行动太早了，但实际上，如果你阻止地区法院的行动，我们基本上现在就能得到我们想要的。
sentences.structure: 第一句：主语从句what they're trying to do + 系动词is + 不定式表语to fudge the request。第二句：主句They're saying，后接直接引语，直接引语中包含but连接的并列句，前一分句含that宾语从句，后一分句含if条件状语从句和what宾语从句。
sentences.analysis: 第一句为典型的主语从句结构。第二句直接引语中，but前后形成对比，if从句表示条件，what从句作get的宾语。

sentences.en: And the reason some of these commonsense Republicans are going, hang on, let's wait a minute, is because a lot of this vote by mail was set up by Republicans to help Republicans.

sentences.structure: 主句：the reason ... is because ...
sentences.analysis: the reason后接定语从句some of these commonsense Republicans are going...，其中going后直接引语作宾语；主句谓语为is，后接because引导的表语从句。

sentences.en: But I think one of the things I want to highlight here is that civil rights groups argue that effectively both the SAVE America Act and the mail-in voting scheme from the executive order would functionally provide an additional burden, right?
sentences.cn: 但我认为我想强调的一点是，民权组织认为，实际上《拯救美国法案》和行政命令中的邮寄投票计划都会在功能上增加额外负担，对吧？
sentences.structure: 主句：I think ...，后接宾语从句one of the things ... is that ...，其中that引导表语从句。
sentences.analysis: 主句I think后省略了that的宾语从句。宾语从句的主语为one of the things，后接定语从句I want to highlight here，系动词is后接that引导的表语从句，表语从句中argue后接that引导的宾语从句。

sentences.en: And so, the question is, what happens next? Do we see a return to hostilities? Is there going to be another round of negotiations between the U.S. and Iran to figure out some kind of long-term arrangement? I imagine that will be top of mind for the prime minister in the White House today.
sentences.cn: 那么，问题是，接下来会发生什么？我们会看到敌对行动再次出现吗？美国和伊朗之间是否会有另一轮谈判来达成某种长期安排？我想这将是今天总理在白宫最关心的问题。
sentences.structure: 第一句：主句the question is，后接直接引语what happens next。第二、三句为一般疑问句。第四句：主句I imagine，后接that引导的宾语从句。
sentences.analysis: 第一句为系表结构，表语为直接引语。第二、三句为独立疑问句。第四句为典型的主谓宾结构，宾语从句中top of mind为固定短语。

sentences.en: It will be extremely valuable for him to have images coming out of the White House of him meeting with the president of United States, positioning himself as a statesman.
sentences.cn: 对他来说，拥有从白宫传出的他与美国总统会面的画面，将自己定位为政治家，将极具价值。
sentences.structure: 主句：It will be extremely valuable for him to have images ...
sentences.analysis: It为形式主语，真正主语为不定式短语to have images...。images后接现在分词短语coming out of the White House作定语，以及of him meeting with...作定语，positioning himself...为伴随状语。

sentences.en: And to see this military campaign against Iran, at least at this point, fail to deliver the desired results is, I think, a significant blow to him, and he'll be doing his best to shore up his foreign policy credentials during this visit.
sentences.cn: 而看到这场针对伊朗的军事行动，至少目前，未能取得预期结果，我认为对他是一个重大打击，他将在这次访问中尽力巩固他的外交政策资历。
sentences.structure: 第一分句：主语And to see this military campaign... fail to deliver...，系动词is，表语a significant blow，插入语I think。第二分句：and he'll be doing his best to shore up...
sentences.analysis: 第一分句为不定式短语作主语，其中fail to deliver为省略to的不定式作宾语补足语（see sb do sth）。第二分句为简单句，将来进行时表示持续动作。

sentences.en: But when we look at what this could mean in the primary, right? And then depending on who you may get for a candidate, that's going to be really interesting if it plays out.
sentences.cn: 但当我们看看这在初选中可能意味着什么，对吧？然后根据你可能得到的候选人是谁，如果真发展到那一步，那将会非常有趣。
sentences.structure: 第一句：时间状语从句when we look at...，其中what引导宾语从句。第二句：现在分词短语depending on...作状语，主句that's going to be really interesting，后接if条件状语从句。
sentences.analysis: 第一句为复合句，look at后接what引导的宾语从句。第二句为简单句，depending on为现在分词短语作条件状语，其中who引导宾语从句。

sentences.en: And so, it's almost as if the two were sort of canceling themselves out. But as Chuck was mentioning, right, she's got the endorsement of also these national figures on the -- from the establishment, right?
sentences.cn: 所以，这几乎就像两者在相互抵消。但正如查克提到的，对吧，她还得到了这些全国性人物——来自建制派的支持，对吧？
sentences.structure: 第一句：主句it's almost as if...，as if引导方式状语从句。第二句：as引导方式状语从句，主句she's got the endorsement...
sentences.analysis: 第一句为系表结构，as if从句使用虚拟语气（were canceling）。第二句as Chuck was mentioning为插入语，主句为简单句。

topics.title: 美以关系与伊朗战争
topics.content: 特朗普与内塔尼亚胡会面，讨论伊朗战争。内塔尼亚胡希望升级战争，而特朗普可能倾向于外交解决。两人关系因黎巴嫩打击和土耳其问题出现紧张。
topics.keywords: 美以关系, 伊朗战争, 内塔尼亚胡, 特朗普, 外交, 升级

topics.title: 美乌关系与俄乌战争
topics.content: 泽连斯基访美寻求反导防御和战略合作，希望获得新制裁。特朗普可能因乌克兰近期胜利而改变态度，劳拉·卢默访乌也影响了MAGA阵营的看法。
topics.keywords: 美乌关系, 俄乌战争, 泽连斯基, 特朗普, 制裁, 反导系统

topics.title: 林赛·格雷厄姆葬礼及其影响
topics.content: 参议员林赛·格雷厄姆的葬礼在华盛顿举行，特朗普致悼词。格雷厄姆是特朗普与外国领导人的关键联络人，其去世可能影响对俄制裁等政策。
topics.keywords: 林赛·格雷厄姆, 葬礼, 特朗普, 制裁, 影响力

topics.title: 欧洲野火危机
topics.content: 法国和西班牙遭遇严重野火，法国出现前所未有的火云现象，西班牙面临史上最大火灾。高温热浪加剧火势，消防员奋力控制。
topics.keywords: 野火, 法国, 西班牙, 热浪, 火云, 污染

topics.title: 日本地震
topics.content: 日本南部发生7.1级地震，导致桥梁倒塌、城堡受损，数千户停电，至少50人受伤，专家警告余震和山体滑坡。
topics.keywords: 日本地震, 7.1级, 倒塌, 停电, 余震

topics.title: 其他新闻
topics.content: 歌手D4vd谋杀案将开庭；萨凡娜·格思里呼吁寻找失踪母亲；俄勒冈州出现冒充ICE官员事件；FAA警告波音737 MAX座椅安装错误；堪萨斯城酋长队教练之子被捕。

topics.title: 美国选举制度与邮寄投票争议
topics.content: 特朗普总统要求最高法院允许其限制邮寄投票的行政命令，并推动参议院通过《拯救美国法案》，甚至不惜废除阻挠议事规则。此举引发共和党内部分歧，参议院多数党领袖约翰·图恩等表示支持废除阻挠议事的票数不足。邮寄投票制度最初由共和党人建立，旨在方便农村选民和海外军人投票，但特朗普认为其易导致舞弊。
topics.keywords: mail-in voting, executive order, filibuster, SAVE America Act, Supreme Court

topics.title: 美国中期选举与党内初选
topics.content: 距离中期选举约100天，民主党在密歇根州参议员初选中出现严重分歧。现任众议员海莉·史蒂文斯获得建制派支持，而阿卜杜勒·埃尔-赛义德得到进步派支持，双方在以色列政策、竞选资金等问题上激烈交锋。共和党则利用民主党内部矛盾，试图将对手描绘为社会主义者。
topics.keywords: midterm elections, primary, Democratic Party, AIPAC, socialism

topics.title: 美以关系与伊朗战争
topics.content: 特朗普总统将与以色列总理内塔尼亚胡会面，这是自美以联合对伊朗发动战争以来的首次会面。内塔尼亚胡面临国内选举压力，希望借会面提升外交形象。然而，伊朗核问题仍未解决，军事行动未达预期效果，双方在下一步行动上存在分歧。
topics.keywords: Israel, Iran, Netanyahu, nuclear, Strait of Hormuz

topics.title: 参议员麦康奈尔的健康问题与透明度
topics.content: 参议院共和党领袖米奇·麦康奈尔上月摔倒后仍在康复中心，未获准返回国会。肯塔基州州长安迪·贝希尔要求麦康奈尔直接向选民证明其履职能力或辞职。此事引发对国会议员年龄、健康透明度以及任期限制的讨论。
topics.keywords: McConnell, health, transparency, term limits, ageism

topics.title: 国会议员对新兴技术的认知差距
topics.content: 资深众议员吉姆·克莱伯恩承认直到一周前才知道ChatGPT，引发对国会议员是否了解人工智能等新兴技术的担忧。随着技术快速发展，立法者需要跟上步伐以制定有效法规。
